prompt:
TASK: CHECK EACH SENTENCE AGAINST THE CLAIMS

You are an adversarial fact checker. Your job is to find every sentence below that says something the CLAIMS do not support. Do not pass a sentence to be agreeable and do not fail one to look diligent. A sentence may read as confident or well written; that is evidence about its writer, not about the claims.

Label every sentence with exactly one of:
- "supported": every factual part of the sentence (each number, each name, each count, each comparison, each cause, each "most", "all", "only" or "none") is stated by one or more of the claims, or follows from them directly with no new number. Give the ids of the claims that together support it.
- "unsupported": any factual part is not stated by the claims, contradicts them, changes a number, drops a qualification a claim carries ("at most", "a bound", "notional", "not established", "candidate"), or states a number no claim states. Say which part, in the reason.
- "no_factual_content": the sentence states nothing that could be true or false about the world: a transition, a statement of what the section will do, a definition of a word the report uses.

The NAMES table maps a code in a claim to the name a sentence uses; a sentence that uses the name is read as if it used the code. A sentence that names a statistical body is checked against the claims for that body.

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per sentence, in order, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:
[{"sentence_id": "S1", "label": "supported", "claim_ids": ["CL-035"], "reason": "one short sentence"}]

NAMES
A12: the check for access policy coherence (An identified, robots-compliant machine client that robots.txt permits is served (not refused by a WAF or bot manager))
A13: the check for discoverability from the product page (A machine client starting from the product page reaches the body's API, its terms, its changelog and its inventory without being told where they are)

CLAIMS
[CL-047] (record) The framework keeps USAFacts' 4 criteria (`A`, `B`, `C`, `D`: accessible, understandable, accurate, open) and adds 3 (`E`, `F`, `G`), for 7 in all.

[CL-046] (record) The framework record holds 50 indicators, 48 in the framework and 2 candidate (`A12`, `A13`), which enters no framework count until the operator adopts it (`DD-054`).
    evidence: note: candidate
    evidence: note: candidate

[CL-078] (prior_art) Structured metadata on a page does not by itself make data usable by machines; discovery, access, interpretation and fitness for use are each required.
    note: Corpus first: manifest title scan and MCP search_text ('fitness for use', 'machine-actionab'); both points are in admitted documents, so no web search was run. Not in the corpus and not searched on the web because the corpus establishes the point: Juran's 'fitness for use' (a book, no fetchable page carries the sentence); OMB's information quality guidelines (the corpus holds the statute, information-quality-act-data-quality-act-sec-515-of-p-l-106, not the guidelines).
    evidence: Wilkinson et al., Scientific Data 3:160018, PDF p. 3, the 'machine actionable' paragraph | quote: "but not capable of parsing it due to it being in an unknown format" | note: The FAIR paper's machine-actionability continuum: an agent must identify an object, judge it useful, judge it usable (licence, consent, access) and act; a machine can reach one step and fail the next.
    evidence: Wilkinson et al., Scientific Data 3:160018, PDF p. 3 | quote: "determine if it is usable, with respect to license, consent"
    evidence: FCSM 19-01, PDF p. 6 | quote: "data quality refers to the data’s “fitness for use” for a user’s own needs" | note: Federal statistical guidance on fitness for use; the same definition is in statistical-policy-working-paper-46-data-quality-assessment and w3c-dwbp-2017 §9 (MCP search_text 'fitness for use', six hits).

[CL-080] (prior_art) Optimizing published content for machine readers has a named discipline, generative engine optimization, which its originators frame as the successor to search engine optimization.
    note: Corpus only; both primary sources are admitted. Further GEO literature in the corpus: martinez-2026-geo-critical-survey, chen-2025-geo-how-to-dominate-ai-search, wu-2025-what-generative-search-engines-like, schulte-2026-dont-measure-once.
    evidence: Aggarwal et al., GEO: Generative Engine Optimization (arXiv 2311.09735), abstract, PDF p. 1 | quote: "we introduce Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), the first novel paradigm"
    evidence: same, §2.2 Generative Engine Optimization, PDF p. 3 | quote: "The advent of search engines led to search engine optimization" | note: The next sentences say traditional SEO methods are not directly applicable to generative engines.
    evidence: llmstxt.org, 'The /llms.txt file', Proposal section | quote: "markdown file to websites to provide LLM-friendly content" | note: The page says the proposal was first written in 2024 and is now at v2.

[CL-081] (prior_art) Publishers increasingly restrict AI crawlers, and the public's access through AI tools depends on those restrictions.
    note: Federal-specific: no measurement of U.S. federal sites' AI-crawler policy was found. Searches: manifest title scan and corpus text grep for 'Longpre', 'Consent in Crisis', 'crawler' (vendor documentation only: cloudflare-ai-crawl-control, rfc-9309, the OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity crawler pages); WebSearch 'study robots.txt AI crawlers blocked federal government .gov websites measurement GPTBot'; read Liu et al., 'Somesite I Used To Crawl' (IMC 2025, cseweb.ucsd.edu), which has no government category; read Ahrefs (above), category-level only.
    evidence: Longpre, S.; Mahari, R.; Lee, A.; et al. | 2024 | Consent in Crisis: The Rapid Decline of the AI Data Commons | abstract | quote: "in a single year (2023-2024) there has been a rapid crescendo of data restrictions" | note: An audit of 14,000 web domains behind C4, RefinedWeb and Dolma; robots.txt and terms of service, longitudinal.
    evidence: OpenAI, Overview of OpenAI crawlers, OAI-SearchBot row | quote: "opted out of OAI-SearchBot will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers"
    evidence: Anthropic support article on its crawlers, Claude-SearchBot row | quote: "may reduce your site's visibility and accuracy in user search results"
    evidence: Stox, P. | 2025 | The AI Bots That ~140 Million Websites Block the Most | body text beside the chart 'AI block rate over time by domain category' | quote: "law & government (42% blocked) sites blocked them more" | note: The nearest thing to a government-specific measure found: a category of about 140 million sites' robots.txt files, with no separation of U.S. federal .gov sites.

[CL-085] (prior_art) The Department of Commerce's definition of AI-ready data and this project's own statement of what it measures are recorded verbatim, side by side.
    note: Prior art since cc_tasks/2026-10-02_commerce_guidance_admission.md: the Commerce definition is now read in its primary source, admitted to the corpus from the FSS policy graph's stored copy (sha256 87068818f5c4c86f1a211cd2375738646ed586c0ca7211d5bd9604636493bd91, equal to the FSS ledger's) and extracted by the standing pipeline into a grounded Definition node. The Commerce text is the Department's guidance glossary, written by its Data Governance Board's Working Group, not a Department-wide regulation. The NOAA order and FCSM 25-03 stay as comparators: NOAA's NAO 216-128 definition shares 'machine-readable and machine-understandable' and adds quality, documentation and access methods; FCSM 25-03 quotes the guidance's aim, not its definition. History: this entry was unsupported on 2026-10-02 because WebFetch of commerce.gov returned HTTP 403 and the prior-art task was not told to check the FSS policy graph, which had held the document since 2026-06-18. The project half is recorded above.
    evidence: Commerce Data Governance Board, Generative Artificial Intelligence and Open Data: Guidelines and Best Practices (v1, 2025-01-16), Appendix A1 Glossary, p. 66; Definition node generative-ai-and-open-data-guidelines-and-best-practices-de::def_ai_ready_data, chunk #c0021, node_asserted at events/batch-023.jsonl:58680 | quote: "AI-ready data: Data that is not just machine-readable, but machine-understandable; data that is enriched with contextual metadata and organized in interpretable standard formats for utilization by AI systems." | note: The glossary entry carries footnote marker 80 after the term, omitted from the quotation. This is the Department's guidance glossary, the document of the Commerce Data Governance Board's AI and Open Government Data Assets Working Group, not a Department-wide regulation or order.
    evidence: Webb, B. | 2026 | DN-005: reorientation. The goal is the framework; L0 is one level of it | DN-005 §1, line 11 | quote: "An AI-readiness framework for federal statistical publishers: a way to rate and score, quantitatively and qualitatively, whether the public and the tools the public now uses can reach, understand and use the data they paid for." | note: The project's own text, quoted whole. The framework record (framework/ai_readiness_framework.json) holds no definition node, so this design note, which CLAUDE.md names as the standing map, is the locator.
    evidence: NAO 216-128, Artificial Intelligence in NOAA, definitions (OCR text corpus/noaa_esip/NAO_216-128.ocr.txt) | quote: "Data that is discoverable, machine-readable and machine-understandable" | note: The definition of 'AI-Ready Data' (the OCR reads 'Al-Ready') continues: 'and has sufficient quality, documentation, and access methods to support the full AI application development and use life cycle'. NOAA is a Commerce bureau; an NAO is a NOAA order, not the Department's definition.
    evidence: FCSM 25-03, PDF p. 3 | quote: "improve accuracy of AI responses and increase the prioritization of its authoritative data" | note: FCSM 25-03 quoting the Commerce guidance's stated aim; this is its purpose, not its definition.

[CL-086] (prior_art) Data buried in aggregated spreadsheets is not machine-usable even when published.
    note: Neither source says 'not machine-usable' in those words: Wickham establishes presentation-layout tables as a common messy form that must be tidied before analysis, and the W3C Recommendation establishes that a format that is not machine-readable limits the data's usefulness. Corpus: DWBP admitted; Wickham not in the corpus (corpus grep 'Wickham', 'tidy data'). data.gov and Federal Data Strategy guidance were not searched: the task says one source suffices.
    evidence: Wickham, H. | 2014 | Tidy Data | §3.1 Column headers are values, not variable names | quote: "A common type of messy dataset is tabular data designed for presentation" | note: Read in the author's copy at the URL; the JSS abstract was confirmed at https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v059i10. §3 lists presentation layouts first among the five most common problems with messy datasets, each needing tidying before analysis.
    evidence: W3C Data on the Web Best Practices, Best Practice 12: Use machine-readable standardized data formats, Why | quote: "Posting data in a format that is not machine-readable places severe limitations" | note: The same paragraph separates formats humans can read and edit on a computer from formats that are machine-readable.

SENTENCES
S1: The framework exists to rate and score, quantitatively and qualitatively, whether the public and the tools the public now uses can reach, understand and use the data they paid for.
S2: The Department of Commerce has set a neighbouring target in its guidance glossary, which defines AI-ready data as data that is not just machine-readable but machine-understandable, enriched with contextual metadata and organized in interpretable standard formats for use by AI systems.
S3: That glossary belongs to guidance written by the Department's Data Governance Board, not to a Department-wide regulation, and read beside the framework's own statement it describes the data, whereas the framework asks whether people and their tools can get to the data and use it.
S4: Publishing data and reaching it are separate problems, because each step between a released file and its use can fail on its own.
S5: Wilkinson and colleagues, setting out the FAIR principles, describe a machine agent that must identify an object, judge it useful, judge it usable with respect to licence, consent and access, and then act, so a machine can complete one step and fail the next.
S6: Structured metadata on a page therefore does not by itself make data usable by machines, since discovery, access, interpretation and fitness for use are each required.
S7: Fitness for use is also the term federal statistical guidance uses for data quality, defined there as fitness for a user's own needs.
S8: For example, figures released in aggregated spreadsheets laid out for presentation are not machine-usable even when published, because a format that machines cannot read places severe limits on what the data can be used for.
S9: Writing for machine readers already has a named discipline, generative engine optimization, which its originators present as the successor to search engine optimization.
S10: The framework keeps 6 of the USAFacts criteria and adds 5 of its own, for 11 in all.
S11: Those machine readers face a further barrier, because publishers increasingly restrict AI crawlers and the public's access to data through AI tools depends on those restrictions.
S12: An audit of 14,000 web domains found a rapid rise in such restrictions within a single year, 2023 to 2024.
S13: The cost of a restriction falls on the public, since OpenAI states that sites opted out of its search crawler will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers, and Anthropic warns that blocking its search crawler may reduce a site's visibility and accuracy in user search results.
S14: However, no measurement of the AI-crawler policies of U.S. federal sites was found, and the nearest measure, drawn from the robots.txt files of about 140 million sites, reports that 42% of law and government sites blocked AI bots without separating U.S. federal sites from the rest.
S15: The framework's structure starts from the 4 criteria USAFacts set out, that data be accessible, understandable, accurate and open, and adds 3 more, for 7 criteria in all.
S16: Below the criteria, the framework record holds 50 indicators, of which 48 are in the framework and 2 are candidates.
S17: Those 2 candidates, the check for access policy coherence and the check for discoverability from the product page, enter no framework count until the framework's operator adopts them.
